speakeroldname: Hon. George C. Nowlan (Minister of National Revenue):
speakerposition: Minister of National Revenue
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION OF CHAIRMAN OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I regret to advise the house that the government has received the resignation of Mr. A. D. Dunton as chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. This resignation was received yesterday afternoon.
Mr. Dunton was appointed chairman of the board in 1945, and from 1945 to the present time he has served in that capacity. It has been, I think we would all agree, one of the most difficult positions in the public service, and he has shown in the administration of that office a combination of tact, firmness and ability which has characterized his term of office and placed the administration on a high level of efficiency which reflects credit on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and on himself. The high standard of C.B.C. radio and the tremendous growth of C.B.C. television culminating in the inauguration of the national microwave system on July 1 will serve as monuments to his record of service to Canada.
Mr. Dunton has received various offers of employment during the last year, all of which he has turned down, but he has been offered one which appeals to him because it provides a different opportunity for public service- one which, I understand, has been tendered to him officially this morning, and which he has accepted, namely, the presidency of Carleton University.
We all regret the fact that his services are lost to the public service of Canada in 57071-3-121J
the field of radio and television, but at the same time we welcome the fact that he is entering another area of public service where he will be able to make a real contribution to the development of this country. His resignation will be effective on July 15.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of Ihe Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION OF CHAIRMAN OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I am sure all hon. members of the house will have heard with great regret the news the minister has just given us of the resignation of one who has served his country with distinction, devotion and intelligence in one of the most difficult positions that any Canadian could hold. Our regret at this news is mitigated to some extent by the other announcement that he is accepting the position as head of one of the two great universities in Ottawa, where he will have further opportunities of public service.

subtopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF RESIGNATION OF CHAIRMAN OF BOARD OF GOVERNORS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it is with great regret certainly that we in this group learn of the resignation of Mr. A. D. Dunton, chairman of the board of governors of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. I believe his resignation is a blow to Canada and to the C.B.C. which has been built up to such great efficiency over the years. Mr. Dunton presided as chairman of the board of governors while the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation was in a state of rapid growth particularly in respect of its television facilities. The corporation has strongly cemented national unity in Canada amongst both our great races and has helped develop a distinctive Canadian culture. Without reservation we are sorry to see Mr. A. D. Dunton resign from this important position. Naturally we are pleased that he will continue to serve his country in another highly important capacity. We wish him health and happiness in his new post, and we anticipate from him the same distinguished service in the years to come.

subtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING PROPOSED REORGANIZATION OF MILITIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in view of the widespread publicity given to the statement I am alleged to have made yesterday that there were to be drastic reductions in the militia,
1908	HOUSE OF
Inquiries of the Ministry and the serious effect and repercussions that may arise from that publicity, I would like to make a brief statement on the actual situation. The question of the reorganization of the militia is now under study along the lines that the organization should be based primarily upon the ability of various localities to support militia units, and partly on the proximity of possible targets for enemy attack.
I still want to stress that the militia is an important element in our deterrent, because it is to be trained so it can help to sustain the life of this nation under a nuclear attack and, therefore, make that attack less effective than if there were no such organization.
There are some localities which experience has shown have not been able to maintain the number of units that had been previously allocated to those localities. Some of these units will have to be amalgamated with others, but there is no drastic reduction contemplated in the militia.

house what concessions have been made by the dominion government to the province of Saskatchewan in connection with the number of acres to be irrigated by the province as a condition of the participation of the dominion government in the South Saskatchewan river dam project?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PROVINCIAL MINISTERS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in reply to this question I think I should refer to a statement made by the Canadian Press and, as such, a statement which affects the privileges of this house. This statement was to the effect that the premier of Saskatchewan had said that the province is "deeply disappointed" that the requested federal government loan to help build the South Saskatchewan river dam had been rejected and accused Prime Minister Diefenbaker of "rank discrimination against Saskatchewan".
If this statement was made by the premier of Saskatchewan, all I can say is that it is in error. The total cost of building a dam up to $100 million will be shared 75 per cent by the federal government and 25 per cent by the provincial government. Of that 25 per cent one-half will be given as a loan by the federal government to the government of Saskatchewan in further assistance with respect to this project.
In so far as concessions are concerned, a very material concession was arrived at as the result of consultation, and that is that while at all times in the past it was understood that if the project was proceeded with 100,000 acres of irrigated land would have to be assured within one year after completion of the dam, we have met the province of Saskatchewan in that regard by reducing by 50 per cent the number of acres subject to irrigation within that period. The other concessions were in general referred to by myself when I brought this matter to the attention of the house on July 2, 1958, and I will not repeat what I said on that occasion.
The premier of Saskatchewan and the minister of agriculture of that province, of course, by their attitudes in this very important matter seem to be generating provincial pre-election schemes.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PROVINCIAL MINISTERS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I think the comment of the Prime Minister has been most regrettable, and I am going to explain why I believe this to be so.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PROVINCIAL MINISTERS
speechtext: Order.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER

made that the Prime Minister had announced that the Saskatchewan application for a loan had been turned down. If that report was on the C.B.C. news is it not possible, though I have no personal knowledge of this, that the report was also in the press in Saskatchewan, and that that was the newspaper report which the premier of that province is answering, just as the Prime Minister himself is answering a news report today?

speakerposition: Prime Minister
subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER
subsubtopic: REFERENCE TO STATEMENTS BY PROVINCIAL MINISTERS
speechtext: That is entirely erroneous, Mr. Speaker. What I was referring to was an additional amount over and above the assistance in the building of the dam, for which the government of Saskatchewan was asking; not assistance in connection with the financing of the dam of which, as I have already stated, we will agree to provide 50 per cent. I am referring now to the one-half of the $25 million on a 20-year debenture basis. Over and above that the premier of Saskatchewan asked that this government should also finance the province's own power development in Saskatchewan, and I said we turned down that proposal. That is a different matter altogether, and there was no erroneous report on the C.B.C.

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER

subtopic: SOUTH SASKATCHEWAN RIVER

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I take this opportunity to answer the question asked yesterday by the hon. member for Nipissing concerning the control of the water level in lake Nipissing. This level, apparently, is very low at the present time, and the hon. member asked whether we could not arrange more effective co-operation measures for control, together with the Ontario hydro commission.
I have now had an opportunity to check this situation with the departmental officials, and I can tell the hon. member that the cooperation between the Ontario hydro and the department is as good as can be, up to the limit that we cannot ask them to seriously endanger their water storage as required for power production needs. Officials of the department have telephone communication always available with officials of the hydro, and both agencies currently exchange information. Hydro also sends to the department weekly and monthly reports on data of discharges and storages.
Hydro have just advised an official of the department that there is no possibility of dumping more water than they have been doing recently. They point out that the Temagami, which is their largest storage, is now two feet below normal, and there is no possibility of dumping any more of the storage water. Spring run-off this year was practically nil, and as a consequence storages are subnormal.
Recently, as a result of some little rain and a high percentage of relative humidity reducing evaporation, the lake level has raised by 0.24 foot. However, unless run-off increases further, water power requirements may necessitate a reduction in discharge at the power dams in view of the present critical situation.
I greatly regret that I cannot give the hon. member a more encouraging report.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to take this opportunity to bring to the attention of the committee a matter which is of the utmost importance to my riding of Kingston and, I believe, of equal importance to the Canadian people. In the planning of the St. Lawrence seaway there was no provision made for the deepening of one small section approximately one-half mile in length at the foot of Wolfe island, some 20 miles east of Kingston. Because there was no provision made for the deepening of this particular section the Canadian channel which has been used almost exclusively since shipping began would no longer be the channel through which the vessels using the St. Lawrence seaway would pass. The western terminal of the St. Lawrence, which has been on the Canadian side of the river, would be transferred to the United States side.
The fact that this channel has been on the Canadian side has made Kingston the pilot's terminal. It has brought industry to this area. It has been responsible for building up shipyard and ship repair facilities which gave to Canadian labour millions of dollars annually in wages. It is obvious that if this one section is not deepened Canadian industry and labour located at the western end of the St. Lawrence river will not only lose the benefits they have enjoyed but will also lose those greater benefits which will result from the building of the St. Lawrence seaway.
It is sound reasoning to believe that ship repair facilities will be required at the junction of the St. Lawrence river and the great lakes. Ships that are damaged in the canals and in the narrow channels to the east of Kingston require repair before proceeding into the open lakes, and ships which suffer damage in the lakes cannot jeopardize the seaway system by proceeding through it without repair. Therefore I suggest that if this one obstacle is allowed to remain and block off the Canadian channel and prevent ships which require repair from reaching the repair facilities now established at Kingston, then these facilities will be built in the United States channel.
The Kingston drydock is owned by the Canadian government. Its cornerstone was laid in 1890 by a Canadian of great vision,
Supply-Public Works Sir John A. Macdonald. It is my hope that this government will take the steps that are necessary to keep in Canada that which we already possess, the western terminal of the St. Lawrence system.
In the early days of this parliament I brought this situation to the attention of the minister. My submissions on behalf of the riding I represent have been enthusiastically and vigorously supported by the Kingston chamber of commerce and by the city council of Kingston. I should like to ask the Minister of Public Works if he and his departmental engineers have had sufficient time to consider my request for the opening of the Canadian channel in this particular area, and, if so, what action the government proposes taking.

We can assure him that we are very conscious of the importance of seeing that the famous old Canadian city of Kingston should not suffer in any way through any lack of action on the part of the government.

Supply-Public Works and lower Duncan rivers. Here again the department will carry out clearance of snags from the upper and lower Duncan rivers to enable it to be used for navigation.

The hon. gentleman also inquired about a wing dam at Arrowhead, British Columbia. The problem at Arrowhead involves the delta made by the Columbia river where it empties into the upper Arrow lakes. This delta is continuing to build and change, and contrary to local public opinion it is not a simple matter of rebuilding a wing dam which satisfied the conditions of some 50 years ago. Two investigations have been carried out in recent years into this problem, and it is the opinion of departmental engineers that a very large expenditure would be required to alleviate the problem at the Arrowhead wharf. My second point is that I would like to know the policy of the department with respect to breakwaters. It is an amazing thing how news travels. People move about more than they used to. A great many of my

constituents who are interested in launch clubs and things of that nature have informed me in rather vigorous terms, as usual, that the department has been in the habit of building breakwaters for launch clubs at Kelowna, Penticton and other points on the Okanagan lakes to protect small boats around the edge of the launch clubs from storms. I would like the minister to explain the policy of his department with respect to the building of breakwaters under those circumstances.
The minister referred to dredging. In fact last year I had 85 craft pass my ranch. The minister knows where I live.

I am told by the commodore of the Seattle yacht club that possibly there will be double that number within the next two years. That shows the necessity for keeping the channels in reasonable shape.
In addition there are two long-term reasons I want to bring to the attention of the minister. When General McNaughton was giving evidence before the external affairs committee with respect to the development of the Columbia river for hydro purpose he mentioned a proposed dam at Murphy creek, and said that because of the great increase in navigation at the present time and the possibility of navigation for the purpose of transporting heavy freight in the future, plans were being made to put locks in any dam that may be built at Murphy creek. I bring that to the minister's attention because it is a long-term point of view. Owing to the rapid industrial development under the Navigable Waters Protection Act there are naturally increasing applications for the building of dolphins and the erection of piles, and also for the extension of works on the banks of the Columbia river and Kootenay lake. While I realize that certain aspects of those applications come under the jurisdiction of the provincial government, navigation comes under the authority of the federal government; and I hope wherever possible

when these applications are made the department will ensure that one of its investigators visits the site and makes certain of the effect of the proposed work and also consults the organizations representing the local people, because irritations can develop quickly due to the fact that all the circumstances surrounding the applications have not been given sufficient consideration.

The result is that the sand and silt dredged out of the slough are silting back in again because of the action of the tide, waves and wind to such an extent that the slough will have to be re-dredged some time in the future.

I am trying very hard to keep out of politics. All I can say about the Ripple Rock blast is that it has been an outstanding
Supply-Public Works success. A survey was made an hour or two after the blast, and it indicated that so much rock had been blasted away by the explosion that at least 47 feet depth of passage had been created between the top of the rock and low water level. Subsequent investigations showed that the larger rock had been cut down to 68 feet below low water level and that the smaller rock had been cut down to 47 feet at least, and probably a little more.
A survey of the currents through the narrows, which have been changed, of course, by the blast, is still not complete, but in so far as the removal of the obstacle itself is concerned, the project has been an outstanding success.

There is a further suggestion I should like to draw to the attention of the minister at this time regarding Seymour Narrows where Ripple Rock used to be. This question has been in the minds of a good number of skippers of ships who have been travelling up and down the inland passage for many years, many of them old-timers who know the coast as well as they know the palms of their hands. They have always felt that Ripple Rock itself was not the danger, but that the danger arose from the turbulence of the currents because of the fact that Ripple Rock was there. Small vessels became caught in these tide swirls and pushed into the shore, and so on. Another difficulty which was encountered many times by steamers and big boats travelling through the Seymour Narrows is this: they discovered that the area for manoeuver, especially in a running tide, was very limited. Running with the tide made things even more difficult. There is a blind corner as you get past the rock southbound, a blind turn in the narrows, and on many occasions they met smaller craft coming up, and the situation was made even more dangerous by the limited area in which they were able to manoeuver, and because of the current.
It has been suggested to me by these skippers-I do not know whether they have made representations through their organization to the department-that some dredging should be undertaken, say, at Maud island- I am not sure of the name-just to the east of Seymour Narrows where there is a gut which over the years has become filled with silt and mud. The suggestion is that this channel should be dredged clean so that it will provide a channel for smaller craft moving up and down the narrows in order that they should not become obstacles to the steamers, freighters and rafts which go up and down there. Such a channel would be an additional safety factor in this particular place.

I do not know whether the minister has been informed that there is a long-standing conflict of jurisdiction concerning the cleaning out of the mouth of the Coquitlam river. At about the time of the first world war the minister's department assumed responsibility because at that time it was a navigable river. The minister knows that the area has now become largely urban and the river is no longer used to any degree for industrial navigation. The mouth of the river has silted so heavily that the level of the river at the mouth has been raised and almost every spring we have a flooding of the city of Port Coquitlam. The city fathers almost every year have made representations to the minister's department as well as to the government of British Columbia and one government shrugs its shoulders and says it is the re-sponbility of the other government.
If my memory serves me correctly the federal authorities argue that since the river is no longer used for navigation their responsibility has ended and that since it is a matter of flood control it is definitely a task falling under the jurisdiction of the provincial government. speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. S-4, ^ respecting the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this bill is to give authority to the shareholders of the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company to authorize, if they so desire, the payment of directors' fees to the directors of the company within the modest limits contained in the bill and also to authorize the reimbursement of expenses incurred by the directors in furthering the company's interests.
Hon. members may like to know who are the directors of this company. They are all well-known west coast gentlemen. One is Alderman Cornett of the city of Vancouver, long experienced in municipal matters; others are Mayor Goldsworthy of the city of North Vancouver and his associate Alderman Gostick; there are also on the board Reeve Sam Macrae and Councillor Fraser of North Vancouver, and Reeve Richards of West Vancouver. Hon. members may also like to know who the shareholders of this company are. Mr. Speaker, the shareholders are as follows: first, there is the city of Vancouver, then the city of North Vancouver, the district of North Vancouver and the municipality of West Vancouver. They own between them some 8,000 shares. These are the total shares outstanding, except 25 additional shares owned by the Cotton estate.
I wish to point out also that the board of directors of this company is charged with the responsibility of operating the company as a profit making company as opposed to, say, a school board or other like institution.

The board has requested that the company charter be amended. Whether or not directors' fees will be paid will finally rest with the municipalities to decide. This bill merely enables fees to be paid. It is up to the shareholders to decide the rest. No director is a shareholder, and thus a director is not entitled to vote unless he acts as proxy. In running this bridge company the directors must give additional time apart from their other duties. They are out to make a profit for the company; it is a commercial business.
I think it might be best if I gave hon. members a short history of this company. The Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company was first incorporated in 1910, giving authority to a private group to build a tunnel in Burrard inlet, Vancouver, British Columbia, at what is known as the first narrows, or a bridge at the second narrows in the same inlet. It was considered at that time that the cost of a tunnel was too great to justify its construction and, in fact, it was too early for the building of a bridge across the second narrows.
The purpose of the bridge was to join the city of North Vancouver, the district of North Vancouver, and the municipality of West Vancouver to the city of Vancouver by roadway. The population of Vancouver at that time was only in the neighbourhood of about 90,000 with the other city and districts very small. Eventually the company's rights of building were taken over by the two cities and two municipalities to which I have referred. The bridge was completed in 1925.
The fixed span of the bridge was carried away in 1930 and replacement was completed in 1934. It was at this time that the federal government made available one million dollars with the proviso that management of the bridge would be assumed by the national harbours board pending the repayment of the loan from the federal government.
Upon the return of the bridge to the bridge company in March 1951 its finances were in extremely bad condition. The company had made default under a trust deed mortgage to the Montreal Trust Company to secure $630,000. No interest had been paid for several years; no sinking fund had been set up for several years, and coupons outstanding in default amounted to $642,600. A similar default existed in regard to a second trust deed mortgage of $70,000. The bridge company had no funds to meet a temporary loan from the national harbours board of $98,000.
The company's financial position had been poor from the time of the construction of its bridge over the second narrows. The supreme court of British Columbia had appointed a
Private Bills
receiver upon the application of the Montreal Trust Company, the trustee under the two bond mortgages.
Under the management of a very able directorate the company's financial situation has greatly improved since March 31, 1951 when the company took over the railway and bridge from the national harbours board.
I have a copy of the company's financial statement for the year ending December 31, 1957, as certified by the company's auditors. The statement shows that the company paid a dividend for the year 1957 of $321,000, being 40 per cent on the capital stock outstanding. The huge amounts of unpaid arrears of interest, coupons and sinking funds referred to have been paid and provided. The company's operating profit before fixed charges for the year ending December 31, 1957, amounted to some $613,000, and after deduction of fixed charges, including depreciation, the company's net profit for the year amounted to some $529,000.
In my opinion, time and ability on the part of the directors will be required in the next few years in excess of the usual time devoted to carrying on the company's business. In view of the construction now proceeding of a competitive bridge at the second narrows, sponsored by the provincial government, I am of the opinion that a new deal with the Canadian National Railways will come up for consideration by the directors of the bridge company. The nature of any new deal cannot be defined now. The formation of it undoubtedly will require considerable study and will require a board of directors sufficiently interested in their work to devote the necessary time and effort. I do not see why they should not receive some reasonable remuneration.
Finally, I mention by way of comparison the fact that members of the greater Vancouver water district, which is a corporation created by provincial statute in 1924, have always been paid. For many years they have been paid-small sums, it is true-but they have received remuneration. The corporation which I have referred to was not constituted for the purpose of making money and paying dividends. The corporation under review at the present time was constituted for making money.
I feel that the directors have been most fair in considering the welfare of the shareholders. The directors could have drafted the bill in such a way as to have provided that they alone could have set the amount to be paid to them by way of remuneration but if hon. members will peruse the draft bill they will see that it is the shareholders and the shareholders only who have the power to determine the amount to be paid.

I should also like to commend the board of directors. As I mentioned, most of them are senior officials in western Canada and most have had long experience in municipal affairs. They have set extremely reasonable sums to be paid as remuneration. They have stipulated that the maximum amount that may be paid to a director shall be the sum of $500 with provision for payment to the president of the sum of $1,200. I am convinced that hon. members will share my feeling that these are most reasonable sums.
The directors are not shareholders of the corporation. They do not even have the right unless appointed as a proxy to be present at the annual meeting. Therefore they do not necessarily have to be at the meeting in order to vote upon this important matter. Such authority is vested solely in the shareholders which, as I explained earlier, are the municipalities concerned. This is an added safeguard over the usual company practice whereby the directors themselves determine the amount of directors fees to be paid. In this instance any fees would have to be authorized by the shareholders meeting which would be composed of persons holding proxies from the shareholder municipalities and, under the Railway Act, such proxies need not be themselves shareholders. Nor is it any requirement whereby a proxy must even be a member of the municipal council. In other words it is quite possible that the directors would not even be present at the shareholders meeting, as I just mentioned, at which the matter of directors fees was determined.
In summary I wish to stress that I feel the directors have acted in good faith, they have drafted a reasonable bill, the sums involved by way of remuneration are not great and there is the added safeguard that the shareholders shall have the right to determine whether or not they shall be paid.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak against the bill as presented by my colleague, the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor). The Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company is a concern which, as has been previously stated, operates a very essential bridge connection between the south shore of Burrard inlet, across the Second Narrows to the north shore. The north shore, I might point out, is one of the major areas represented in my riding of Coast-Capilano. The bulk of the ownership of this company is likewise represented by holdings held by the municipalities on the north shore. Sixty per cent of the shareholdings are held by the city of North Vancouver and the municipal district of North Vancouver. The small amount of the balance entitles the municipality of West 
Vancouver to seat one director on the board of this company and also to participate in its control to a very small degree. The city of Vancouver itself holds a small share interest and is entitled to the seating of one director on the board.
On the surface it would appear that the purpose of this bill is in order and in keeping with normal, good business practice. However, as the mover has pointed out, since the incorporation of the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company in 1910, some 48 years ago, it has had a checkered and quite colourful career. Indeed, in the earlier years it was out of operation more than it was in operation. This has been a matter which has direly affected the life and interest of the people living in the north shore area. For a great many years, other than for ferry contact, it provided the only access to the north side of Burrard inlet.
It is faulty and quite incorrect to consider that it was established and eventually controlled by the municipal areas on the north shore for the purpose of making a profit. It was established for and has been administered by the municipality and city council of North Vancouver for the sole purpose of providing access to the north shore area. Its administration by its directors falls well into the category of a normal operation through a council of aldermen or councillors being named to committees to administer this public utility. The subject of its operation has formed the basis of active and heated debate throughout the more populated area of my constituency, not for just a few years but for many years.
I think it is important to point out the matter of its earning power at this time. Much has been said about the management of the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company. I wish to pay tribute to those who have been appointed by the three councils and the council of the city of Vancouver in connection with the operation of this essential public utility. However, I wish to stress the fact that its earning power at this time has developed only through the tremendous increase in population in the three municipalities it services on the north shore. It is by virtue of the bridge tolls paid by the taxpayers of that area that those revenues are garnered. The taxpayers of these communities are the very people who for well over two and a half decades have been called upon, through tax assessments, to pay deficits on the operation of this bridge company. The load has fallen heavily on the people living in Coast-Capilano. They are, as has been pointed out, the shareholders, and in the

course of the last seven years these shareholders have protested vigorously on two grounds.
One is that council should be able to appoint a man from their midst to act on what virtually is a municipal committee and receive remuneration denied a committee man serving on other essential jobs while in office and a member of council. They have also strongly voiced the opinion that any revenues garnered from the operation of the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company represent basically overcharges placed upon the citizens of the north shore and are a clear indication that rather than operating on a profit basis the bridge tolls should be reduced.
Further to these factors, I would like to point out that if after this strange interim period, being almost 48 years of history, this company shows large profits, those profits are entirely of a temporary nature since a new second narrows bridge, which has already been mentioned and which suffered dire damage and was the scene of a great disaster in my area not many weeks ago, is under construction. It is a 6-lane high level structure. When it is completed, certainly in a period of not more than three years from now, the second narrows bridge will again face financial disaster and the people who will be obliged then to pay for this administration charge if now permitted will be the citizens of my constituency. Mr. Speaker, they have protested and I support them in their protest.
Further, I submit that in three years time this company will be faced with very serious and tragic deficiencies, and I trust that it will be possible through discussions with our federal Department of Transport to see that the old second narrows bridge span, which must be kept in service, as it will still remain at the time of the opening of the service of the new second narrows bridge, as the only carrier of rail traffic, is again brought under the control of the harbours board to form the first portion of an integrated harbours board rail connection and distribution system throughout the north and south sides of Burrard inlet.

As a result of the mistake made by the people constructing the bridge, the steamship Eurana struck the bridge in March, 1927 and a 300 foot span was thrown into Burrard inlet.
This resulted in a very interesting case which went to the privy council, the Steamship Eurana vs the Burrard Inlet Tunnel and Bridge Company. It is reported in 1931 Appeal Cases at page 300. If I may be permitted, sir, I should like to read the head-note in that case.

Where a special act of the dominion legislature has authorized the construction of a bridge carrying a railway over a navigable channel "so as not to interfere with navigation", and has incorporated the Railway Act, an order made by the railway board under section 268 of that act, which empowers the board to authorize the construction of a bridge over navigable waters according to plans approved by the governor in council, affords no defence to a claim in respect of damage caused to a ship by reason of the bridge constructed being a substantial interference with navigation and therefore a public nuisance. Although the hon. member for Vancouver-Burrard (Mr. Taylor) gave us an excellent dissertation on the background of this particular bill, at no time did he state that the councils of the respective municipalities were in unanimous agreement that this remuneration be paid to the directors. I feel that I cannot support the bill until I am assured that the municipalities are giving their wholehearted support to it.
I am not inquiring as to the position taken by any member of the council, but we are rather in this position where the directors are suggesting the granting of an increase to themselves, and in all likelihood the municipal councillors will be the individuals who will be receiving the proxies from the municipalities so they will, in effect, be voting this amount of money to themselves. In view of the relatively small amount, which is approximately $1,200 for the president, who is also a director, and the $500 a year for the other directors, I cannot see the necessity for this bill. If it is felt that the directors should receive remuneration, I would be glad to give my whole-hearted support on the basis that, first of all, the councils give a unanimous indication they are supporting this measure.

Yes; I thank the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch). I would support it on the basis that the councillors give their whole-hearted support as shareholders to the idea of these payments and, secondly, I would go so far as to say that the amount to be paid to the directors would be unlimited. Then the municipalities would have the discretion as to the amount to be paid.

I have risen to speak on this measure because I feel that the councillors and municipalities are performing a public service, and we will have a situation where one or two members of the council will become directors and therefore entitled to extra remuneration as compared with the other members of the council. I feel that this will breed a sense of inequality, and take away from the finer service functions which the councillors perform. I feel, therefore, for the reasons I have stated, and because of the reservations I have made, I cannot support this bill.

subtopic: BURRARD INLET TUNNEL AND BRIDGE COMPANY

Mr. Speaker, as a result of the excellence of the arguments that have already been put forward, I shall have very little to say. I think you will have noted that this is the first time for many long years that a private bill has really been considered as a private bill by the members of this house. Thus far, we have had one member speaking on behalf of the bill and two members of the same political party opposing the bill. I feel that this attitude towards private bills is to be heartily welcomed. I say that this is unique, at least over the past number of years.
I,	like the member for Vancouver East (Mr. Winch) was very surprised indeed at being faced with this bill at the present time. I have not heard of any representation made by the city of Vancouver, the district of North Vancouver or the district of West Vancouver for endorsation of the principle of this bill. I feel there is a vital principle involved in that one appointee of a municipal council is going to be placed in a preferred position over other appointees. When I think of the appointee of a council to a hospital board I immediately realize that that appointee has more work to do, has far greater responsibility and-certainly over the last few years-has had much more anxiety than has the appointee representing the council on this bridge company's board.
I very much regret this bill has come before us in this manner. I find it almost beyond my ability to vote against a request made by public servants, especially municipal servants. I do not like to vote against the principle of the bill until I have had the chance to examine it much more closely and it is for that reason that I move:
That the bill be not now read a second time but that the subject matter thereof be referred to the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines.
We in this group have a tremendous respect for our municipally elected officers and I do not like to vote against something for which they have asked without having

thoroughly convinced myself that the principle is in fact wrong. If it is wrong we would, of course, have to vote against it but if we find the principle is not as we imagine it to be we shall be most happy to support the bill when it comes before this House of Commons for second reading.

First of all, we have heard from two previous speakers of their concern for the taxpayers. I realize, of course, that it is the duty of every one of us to protect the interests of the taxpayers but, at the same time, I feel if these directors are entitled to remuneration for the job they are doing, if they are earning that pay, this argument on behalf of the taxpayers is not a legitimate one. If they are doing a good job they are entitled to remuneration.

What we must find out is whether they are so entitled and in looking back over the history of the legislation I find in the early days of its existence provision was made for the payment of directors in such a case. Perhaps the mover of the bill might let us have some information on this aspect of the matter because somewhere along the line, in connection with the amendment as to who would comprise the board of directors, that particular provision seems to have been dropped.
I have looked back over all the discussions which have taken place with respect to this act since its inception in 1910 and I cannot find any particular reason as to why this provision was dropped. 1.	Is there a travelling establishment committee or a complement committee for the Department of National Defence which makes periodic inspections of national defence establishments and which recommends decreases or increases in (a) civil service staffs; (b) civilian prevailing rate employees?
2.	If so, how many members comprise this committee and what departments do they represent?
3.	At what intervals does this committee make inspections and are the inspections made on the ground at each establishment?
4.	When will the next inspections be made at (a) Renous naval ammunition depot; (b) Chatham R.C.A.F. station; (c) St. Margarets R.C.A.F. station, New Brunswick?
Answer by: Hon. G. R. Pearkes (Minister of
National Defence):
1.	Yes.
2.	Each of the three services has its own establishment or complement committee. The personnel of these committees varies as between the three services, but all contain a representative of the deputy minister's office, and a representative of the civil service commission staff. These committees make recommendations regarding numbers and categories of both service and civilian personnel. The recommendations of these service establishment or complement committees regarding increases or decreases in the numbers of civilian positions, both annual salaried and prevailing rate, are considered by the Department of National Defence and the civil
service commission before the Minister of National Defence formally requests treasury board action to amend establishments.
3.	There is no fixed interval for making establishment reviews, although such reviews are normally conducted at intervals of two to three years. In some cases, on the ground inspections are made by investigators who report to the committee; in other cases, such inspections are carried out by one or more members of the committee; in still others, on the ground inspections are not deemed to be necessary.
4.	(a) Autumn 1959; (b) a study was carried out at this station in May of this year and it is anticipated that a further study will be made in 1960; (c) summer 1958.
